note.p: The Boinville family had a long association with the Godwins. John Baptiste Boinville’s father-in-law, John Collins, had been involved in Godwin’s and Marshall’s ventures in the 1780s in the West Indies (see MS Abinger, 1784 letters). In 1793 Jean Baptiste eloped with Harriet Collins to Gretna Green, Scotland. He remarried her across the border in England, at the insistence of her father, to ensure the legality of any heirs. The couple had two children: Cornelia Boinville born in 1793 and Alfred Boinville born in 1795 (see biography of Harriet Boinville, 17-19; 25-26, 33).

Like his wife, Harriet Boinville, Jean Baptiste admired Godwin. Cornelia Newton and John Frank Newton (his wife’s sister and brother-in-law) were also fervent Godwinians (St. Clair, 263). Jean Baptiste’s important role in the French Revolution was closely connected to General Lafayette. He served as his aide-de-campe in the Paris National Guard and later went to London for him on a secret diplomatic mission (see Cameron, 244-245). While Lafayette was imprisoned in Austria for five years, Jean Baptiste was among the people who tried, without success, to win his release. He was freed in 1797 by Napoleon’s advancing armies. Jean Baptiste is mentioned by name in a letter of thanks Lafayette wrote from prison, now preserved in George Washington’s papers (see biography of Harriet Boinville, 38; Shelley and His Circle, III: 276).

Jean Baptiste used Boinville (rather than Chastel de Boinville) the last name used by later generations of the family. See the memoir of his grandson Charles (Constable) as well as the letter Jean Baptiste wrote his compatriot Alexandre d’Arblay (MS Berg), congratulating him on his marriage to the writer Frances Burney. In 1810 and again in 1812, Jean Baptiste assisted Frances Burney d’Arblay in her efforts to leave Paris and return to England (see biography of Harriet Boinville, 62-63, 65-67; and Burney, 154, 133, 167). Jean Baptiste crossed the Channel many times during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Appointed Directeur de Vivres in Napoleon’s army, with responsibilities for provisioning the troops, he died after the retreat from Moscow as a prisoner-of war (Shelley and His Circle, 276).
